Not in the way it used to. Google removed the "Cached" links from search results in early 2024 and later that year disabled the cache function entirely — the `cache:` operator no longer returns a saved page either. Search Liaison Danny Sullivan confirmed the change, explaining the feature existed for an era when pages often failed to load, and that reliability has since improved enough to make it unnecessary. Reporting at the time also noted the storage cost of keeping snapshots of essentially the whole web was a likely factor.

Worth separating two things, though: Google still crawls and stores page content internally — that's how indexing works, and it's why a search snippet can sometimes show text that's already been edited off the live page. What's gone is *public access* to that stored copy.

Alternatives depending on what you need:

- **Wayback Machine** (archive.org/web) — the main replacement for viewing historical versions. Coverage is patchier than Google's was, but it goes back much further.
- **archive.today** — often catches pages the Wayback Machine misses, and handles some sites more reliably.
- **Search Console URL Inspection** — if it's your own site, this shows you exactly how Google crawled and rendered the page, which is what most SEO people actually wanted the cache for.

One casualty worth mentioning: researchers and journalists who used the cache to track quietly deleted or altered content lost a tool with no direct equivalent, since archives only have a page if someone or something captured it beforehand.

Google will no longer be keeping a backup of the entire Internet. Google Search's "cached" links have long been an alternative way to load a website that was down or had changed, but now the company is killing them off. Google "Search Liaison" Danny Sullivan confirmed the feature removal in an X post, saying the feature "was meant for helping people access pages when way back, you often couldn't depend on a page loading. These days, things have greatly improved. So, it was decided to retire it."

The feature has been appearing and disappearing for some people since December, and currently, we don't see any cache links in Google Search. For now, you can still build your own cache links even without the button, just by going to "https://webcache.googleusercontent.com/search?q=cache:" plus a website URL, or by typing "cache:" plus a URL into Google Search. For now, the cached version of Ars Technica seems to still work. All of Google's support pages about cached sites have been taken down.

Cached links used to live under the drop-down menu next to every search result on Google's page. As the Google web crawler scoured the Internet for new and updated webpages, it would also save a copy of whatever it was seeing. That quickly led to Google having a backup of basically the entire Internet, using what was probably an uncountable number of petabytes of data. Google is in the era of cost savings now, so assuming Google can just start deleting cache data, it can probably free up a lot of resources.

Not in the way it used to. Google removed the "Cached" links from search results in early 2024 and later that year disabled the cache function entirely — the `cache:` operator no longer returns a saved page either. Search Liaison Danny Sullivan confirmed the change, explaining the feature existed for an era when pages often failed to load, and that reliability has since improved enough to make it unnecessary. Reporting at the time also noted the storage cost of keeping snapshots of essentially the whole web was a likely factor.

Worth separating two things, though: Google still crawls and stores page content internally — that's how indexing works, and it's why a search snippet can sometimes show text that's already been edited off the live page. What's gone is *public access* to that stored copy.

Alternatives depending on what you need:

- **Wayback Machine** (archive.org/web) — the main replacement for viewing historical versions. Coverage is patchier than Google's was, but it goes back much further.

The short answer is: **it depends on the type of contract and the data involved**, but for most federal contractors — especially defense contractors — annual cyber awareness training is effectively required. Here's a breakdown:

---

**For DoD / Defense Contractors (NIST SP 800-171 & CMMC)**

This is where the clearest annual training requirement exists. NIST SP 800-171 requires all employees to complete a dedicated annual cybersecurity awareness training, with the goal of 100% completion at least once every 365 days. This applies to contractors handling **Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI)**.

The Awareness and Training (AT) control family under NIST 800-171 covers providing security awareness training to all users, training personnel on recognizing and reporting insider threats, and providing role-based security training to individuals with specific security responsibilities.

Best practice guidance recommends requiring information system users to complete this training when first hired and annually thereafter.

---

**CMMC Framework (Now in Effect)**

As of November 10, 2025, a final DoD rule amending the DFARS incorporates the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) program into DoD contracts. Under CMMC:

- CMMC Level 1 (for contractors handling Federal Contract Information) requires an annual self-assessment following 15 security requirements from FAR Clause 52.204-21. Level 2 (for those handling CUI) maps to NIST SP 800-171 and includes yearly affirmations of compliance.

---

**For Non-DoD Federal Contractors**

The requirement is less uniform but trending toward broader application. On January 15, 2025, the FAR Council published a proposed FAR CUI Rule that would standardize and extend cybersecurity requirements to all federal contractors, not just those working with DoD. This rule is still being finalized.

---

**Key Nuances**

- The *specific* word "annual" is not always spelled out in the regulations themselves — rather, the underlying NIST controls (AT.L2-3.2.1 through 3.2.3) mandate ongoing, documented awareness training, which industry practice and assessors interpret as annual.
- NIST 800-50 itself is guidance, not a standalone law, but the security awareness and role-based training obligations it implements are mandatory under CMMC/NIST SP 800-171 for defense contractors handling CUI.
- Requirements vary by contract type, the sensitivity of information handled, and which clauses (DFARS, FAR 52.204-21, etc.) are included in the contract.

**Bottom line:** If you're a DoD contractor handling CUI, annual cyber awareness training is a firm compliance requirement. For other federal contractors, strong guidance and emerging regulations point in the same direction, even if the exact cadence isn't always codified as "once per year" in statute.

The Procurement Technical Assistance Program was established to expand the number of businesses capable of participating in government contracts. The program is administered by DLA's Office of Small Business in cooperation with states, local governments and nonprofit organizations. Under the program, Procurement Technical Assistance Centers (PTACs) help businesses pursue and perform under contracts with the Department of Defense, other federal agencies, state and local governments and with government prime contractors. Most of the assistance the PTACs provide is free. PTAC support to businesses includes registration in systems such as the System for Award Management (SAM), identification of contract opportunities, help in understanding requirements and in preparing and submitting bids. Professional setup fees to become DCAA-compliant before your first government contract ($10,000–16,000), specifically including attorney fees to establish a Section 409A deferred compensation plan required under FAR 31.205-6 and CPA fees to set up a DCAA-compliant accounting system. content.text:
Good context to have. ECDI is a CDFI — Community Development Financial Institution — which means they're a nonprofit, mission-driven lender designed specifically for businesses that can't easily access traditional bank financing. They're more flexible than a bank and often work with startups. They offer loans from $750 to $2 million with terms up to six years, and they're an SBA microloan intermediary, which means up to $50,000 through that program.

One important logistics note: any owner with more than 20% equity must apply. Both you and your co-founder at 67%/33% both exceed that threshold, so you'll each pay the $25 application fee and both need to be prepared for these questions.

Here's how to think through each one based on everything we've covered.

---

**1. How much do you need to finance?**

With the deferred compensation plan in place, your founders' salaries don't create an immediate cash need. What does create a cash need is everything that can't be deferred:

- Attorney fees (plan document, board consent, employment agreements): $2,500–5,700
- CPA fees (DCAA accounting system, CAS 415, indirect rates): $3,700–10,500
- Health insurance first month premiums: $1,400–2,300
- Software and operational setup: $500–1,000
- Workers' comp deposit: $200–500
- Business insurance: $500–1,000
- Working capital buffer to cover mandatory costs during the government payment gap: $10,000–15,000

A well-grounded ask is $25,000–$35,000. The SBA microloan cap through ECDI is $50,000, so you have headroom. Don't ask for more than you can justify specifically — CDFIs respond better to precise, well-documented needs than to round numbers.

---

**2. What will the funds be used for?**

Be specific and organized. Something like:

Professional setup fees to become DCAA-compliant before your first government contract ($10,000–16,000), specifically including attorney fees to establish a Section 409A deferred compensation plan required under FAR 31.205-6 and CPA fees to set up a DCAA-compliant accounting system. Working capital ($10,000–15,000) to cover mandatory operating costs during the gap between contract start and first government payment — specifically health insurance premiums, software, and operational expenses that cannot be deferred under the compensation arrangement. A specific, itemized use-of-funds statement will strengthen the application significantly.

---

**3. How much equity will you be putting in? (Minimum 12%)**

This is the question that conflicts with your earlier stated preference not to put in personal capital. The math on 12% equity:

If you borrow $35,000 and that's 88% of total project cost, total project is roughly $39,800 and your equity injection is approximately $4,800.

That's a much smaller number than "personal capital" might have implied earlier. It's worth reconsidering whether $4,000–5,000 is something you can manage — particularly if pre-incorporation expenses you've already paid (attorney consultations, research, software, prior professional fees) can be documented and counted toward the equity injection. Ask Catherine specifically whether already-incurred pre-incorporation expenses qualify. If they do, you may already be close to or at the 12% threshold.

---

**4. Are you on a strict timeline?**

Yes, but the timeline is event-driven rather than calendar-driven. You need the funds in place before you sign your first contract, because the DCAA-compliant accounting system and legal documents must be established before the first day of contract performance. You can't predict the exact date a contract will be awarded, but you know you cannot sign without the infrastructure funded and in place. Frame it as: you have an active proposal pipeline and need to be ready to execute when an award comes. That's a more compelling answer than a specific date.

---

**5. Do you have a business plan with financial projections, or 2 years of tax returns?**

As a startup, you have no tax returns. You need a business plan with financial projections. Based on everything we've discussed, yours should include:

- Company description and services (cognitive models, DARPA-type R&D work)
- Management team bios (your background, co-founder's background)
- Target market (DoD agencies, DARPA BAAs, cost-reimbursable contracts)
- Revenue projections: year 1 single CPFF contract at $400–500K
- Cost structure: direct labor, fringe rate (~18–20%), G&A rate (~10%)
- Cash flow projections showing the government payment timing gap and how the loan bridges it
- Year 2 projections showing second contract and growing revenue

If you don't have this written yet, it's worth preparing before the meeting. The SBDC at the Entrepreneurs Center (937-210-9460) offers free help building a business plan and financial model — worth a call before your ECDI meeting if time allows.

---

**6. What monthly payment are you comfortable with?**

At $35,000 over five years at a typical CDFI rate (CDFIs often run 7–10%):

- At 8%: approximately $709/month
- At 10%: approximately $744/month

At $25,000 over five years:
- At 8%: approximately $507/month
- At 10%: approximately $531/month

On a $400K contract billing at a fully-burdened rate, $500–750/month is very manageable once government payments start arriving. The honest answer is that you're comfortable with $500–750/month once you're under contract, but that pre-contract you have minimal cash flow. Ask Catherine whether ECDI offers a payment deferral for the first few months — some CDFIs do, particularly for startups that are pre-revenue at the time of the loan. The Ohio Micro-Loan Program she may also offer has 0% interest — worth asking whether you qualify for that program specifically.

---

**7. What does your credit look like?**

This one only you can answer. A few things worth knowing:

CDFIs are more flexible than banks on credit. ECDI specifically serves businesses that can't access traditional financing, so imperfect credit doesn't disqualify you. What they care most about is willingness to repay and a credible plan for cash flow.

If there are any late payments or collections in your history, disclose them proactively with brief explanations. Lenders respond better to transparency than to surprises in the credit pull. A score above 650 opens most CDFI programs; above 700 gets you better rates.

Both founders' credit will be reviewed since you both exceed the 20% ownership threshold.

---

**One thing to ask Catherine**

Whether there's a program specifically for businesses pursuing government contracts. Some CDFIs have contract-specific loan programs with terms tied to contract performance rather than standard monthly repayment schedules — meaning payment is structured around when you receive government invoices. If ECDI has this, it solves the timing problem more elegantly than a standard monthly repayment loan.
